title: The training principles series: warming up & stretching
summary: He argues pre-workout static stretching is a waste of time and an injury risk on cold tissue; static stretching after training is fine, and he keeps only post-workout hip flexor stretches due to desk work and hanging leg raises. The best warm-up is the lift itself ramped up from light weight with high reps; he always starts bench with an empty bar after a past pec strain. Warm-up needs are individual and affect programming, and time saved matters because naturals need so much volume.

claims.claim: He did lots of static stretching before and after practice over five years of team sports and carried the habit into lifting at first.
Static stretching before training does nothing useful, may hurt performance, and is an injury risk because you're elongating cold muscles and tendons.
He has seen people tear hamstrings doing straight-leg toe touches to get more flexible.
When he stopped stretching before training nothing changed (no more injuries, no lost strength or reps) except that he saved time.
If you stretch before lifting, try two weeks without it and assess; if you love a particular pre-lift stretch, keep it.
Static stretching after lifting is different because muscles are warm and less susceptible to injury.

The only stretches he still does are post-workout hip flexor stretches, because sitting for long periods at work tightens them and that can impair squats and deadlifts and strain the lower back through the kinetic chain.
Hanging leg raises make tight hips worse; if he skips hip stretching for a week, he feels it.
Dynamic stretching before training is valid, but the easiest way is to do the exercise itself with lighter weights to pump blood into the area.
Example bench warm-up: empty bar for 30 reps, then 25s per side for 20 reps, then 45s per side for 10 reps, with jumps chosen to suit you.

He once got a bad pec strain from starting bench at 135 without warming up and feared he'd need surgery; it healed on its own, and now, though he benches in the 200s, he always starts with an empty bar then 25-30 reps with 25s on.
High-rep warm-ups pre-fatigue the muscle, but for a bodybuilder that doesn't really matter.
Even squatting in the high 300s he starts with 25s on the bar; for deadlift he starts heavier because he's never had lower back issues. Apply warm-up principles to your own body.
He used to do band chest activation and plate shoulder warm-ups but stopped because jumping straight to the empty bar works just as well.
Natural bodybuilders eventually need so much volume that any 10 minutes saved is critical, worth about two extra quality sets.
He sees no benefit to warming up with cardio; ramping up the lift is enough. Start with layers like a hoodie so you're sweating by your working sets.
Warm-up time is individual and reportedly longer for older lifters; his knees and back take a long time for squats while he can jump straight into deadlifts.
Warm-up time affects programming: if warming up for squats took 45 minutes, squatting daily would waste a lot of time.
